provenance.source_title: The water footprint of artificial intelligence: Emerging solutions and governance imperatives

content.reading_plan: This is a short, densely referenced Water Research “Making Waves” article: a narrative review that combines technical explanation, reported consumption figures, facility examples, and policy advocacy. I will follow its sections in order, generally taking a few paragraphs or one technical subsection per step, slowing down for definitions, numerical comparisons, and trade-offs. The prepared text contains an interrupted methodological passage; I will identify that interruption rather than treat it as an argumentative transition. I will read Table 1 with its retained image to preserve its column structure and qualifications.

reading_path.location: Opening highlights and abstract
reading_path.moves: Problem framing; summary claims; announcement of a governance concept and policy position.

claims.text: AI’s environmental footprint is assessed mainly through electricity use and greenhouse-gas emissions, leaving water a less visible dimension.
AI infrastructure consumes freshwater through evaporative cooling, electricity generation, and semiconductor manufacturing.
Projections suggest AI's global water footprint could reach 4.2–6.6 billion cubic meters annually by 2027.
Two-thirds of post-2022 data centers are located in water-stressed regions.
Cold-climate siting, natural-water-body cooling, waterless designs, and waste-heat recovery can reduce on-site demand, but deployment remains limited.
“Digital water sobriety” links judgments about which AI applications justify freshwater consumption with water-conscious siting and mandatory facility-level transparency.
Achieving water-sustainable AI demands not merely technological optimization but fundamental policy reform integrating water constraints into computational infrastructure planning.

reading_path.meaning: The opening presents water as an overlooked material requirement of seemingly digital activity. It also establishes the article’s normative perspective: efficiency is not the only issue; the justification, location, and accountability of resource use matter. These are introductory announcements rather than arguments yet developed.

reading_path.location: Section 1, opening three paragraphs
reading_path.moves: Contrast between user experience and infrastructure; quantitative illustration; decomposition of the footprint; scope restriction.

claims.text: AI appears intangible and effectively costless to users, while every conversation, image generation, and model-training run produces waste heat at distant data centers that often requires water-intensive cooling.
The water consumption associated with AI is substantial.

support.text: Li et al. estimate approximately 700,000 liters of clean freshwater for GPT-3 training and the equivalent of a 500 ml bottle for 10–50 medium-length responses.

citations.reference_entry: Li, X., Ren, S., Arlington, U., 2024. Addressing the water footprint of artificial intelligence: a path towards sustainability. arXiv preprint arXiv: 2304.03271v5..

support.text: Conditional on continued growth in AI use, the cited projections put annual global AI water footprint at 4.2–6.6 billion cubic meters by 2027 and U.S. data-center consumption at up to 280 billion liters annually by 2028.

claims.text: The footprint comprises direct cooling and humidification consumption, indirect water use in electricity supply, and water embedded in chip manufacturing, where fabrication consumes thousands of liters per wafer.

support.text: The paragraph cites a discussion of data centers and water consumption for its three-part account.

claims.text: This work focuses on operational water consumption for cooling, as it constitutes the most substantial and directly manageable portion.

reading_path.meaning: The introduction develops the opening’s visibility problem through familiar user activities and concrete volumes. It then narrows a three-component environmental footprint to operational cooling, explicitly justifying that selection by magnitude and manageability.

reading_path.location: Section 1, paragraph beginning “While all data centers” and concluding paragraph
reading_path.moves: Comparison; causal explanation; differentiation of AI from conventional computing; inference to a need for dedicated assessment.

claims.text: AI workloads, especially accelerated-server workloads, demand more computational power, consume more electricity, generate more heat, and therefore require advanced cooling.

support.text: The author invokes the United States Data Center Energy Usage Report for the workload-to-energy-to-cooling relationship.

claims.text: AI training runs operate at near-100% GPU utilization continuously for weeks or months, unlike variable transactional workloads; this eliminates cooling downtime and maximizes cumulative training-period water consumption.
Hyperscale AI facilities concentrate water demand at individual sites far beyond traditional distributed enterprise computing, amplifying local water stress.

support.text: The author compares AI rack power densities of 50–100+ kW with 5–10 kW in conventional enterprise facilities, and says one hyperscale training site can concentrate the water demand of dozens of smaller conventional centers.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California. LBNL2001637. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/32d6m0d1. accessed 06.12.25.

claims.text: These distinctions establish that AI infrastructure presents a qualitatively different water challenge from general-purpose cloud computing, warranting dedicated assessment and mitigation strategies.

reading_path.meaning: The discussion moves from the existence of a water footprint to the reason for treating AI separately. The conclusion depends on three linked characteristics—intensity, sustained utilization, and concentration—rather than on total volume alone.

reading_path.location: Section 2, review-method passage, including its continuation printed after the Section 3 heading
reading_path.moves: Method description; source hierarchy; disclosure of review rather than original calculation.

claims.text: The evidence synthesis uses a targeted review of peer-reviewed studies found through Web of Science and Google Scholar for 2015–2025, corporate sustainability and technical reports, and investigative journalism and policy analyses.

The peer-reviewed stream prioritizes quantitative assessments and lifecycle analyses; corporate sources cover Google, Microsoft, and AWS practices and metrics; journalism and policy sources document siting conflicts, regulation, and community impacts.
Peer-reviewed sources were prioritized over the other two sources.
This work does not perform an independent water footprint calculation; rather, it synthesizes quantitative data as reported in the reviewed literature and corporate disclosures.

reading_path.meaning: The author explains how heterogeneous evidence enters the review and gives peer-reviewed work priority. The prepared text splits the review-method sentence across the Section 2 opening and the material following the Section 3 heading; read together, these fragments describe one method, not a change of subject.

reading_path.location: Section 2, water-footprint definitions and scope qualifications
reading_path.moves: Definition; distinction between measurements; introduction of scarcity weighting; limitation of scope and data comparability.

claims.text: The water-footprint framework, formally standardized in ISO 14046, distinguishes blue water, green water, and grey water: surface and groundwater consumption, rainwater stored in soil, and the volume needed to assimilate pollutants.

support.text: The author grounds the terminology in water-footprint and life-cycle-assessment literature.

claims.text: The review focuses on operational blue water consumed or evaporated on-site for cooling, quantified through WUE, but most figures it cites reflect withdrawals unless otherwise specified because reporting often conflates withdrawal and consumption.
A comprehensive assessment of green and grey water, scarcity-weighted impacts, and indirect electricity and semiconductor water lies beyond this review’s scope and remains a research priority.

reading_path.meaning: This passage places important boundaries around the earlier figures. The nominal focus is consumption, but the available evidence often measures withdrawal. It also separates low consumptive volume from absence of ecological impact and introduces place-sensitive assessment without claiming to perform it.

reading_path.location: Section 3, WUE definition; Table 1 and its footnotes
reading_path.moves: Metric definition; comparative tabulation; qualification of estimates and system boundaries.

claims.text: WUE is annual site water used for cooling and humidification divided by annual IT energy consumption, expressed in liters/kWh or m³/MWh.

support.text: The definition is attributed to an explanation of WUE in data centers.

claims.text: Fully air-cooled facilities approach zero WUE, while heavily evaporative facilities may exceed three m³/MWh depending on climate and system design.

support.text: The author cites the U.S. data-center energy report for this range.

reading_path.location: Section 3.1, Cooling technologies and their water implications
reading_path.moves: Mechanistic comparison; conditional explanation; identification of burden shifting.

claims.text: Cooling architecture and local climate primarily determine AI-intensive data centers’ water footprints.

support.text: Evaporative and adiabatic systems combine high energy efficiency with high WUE; air cooling minimizes on-site water while increasing electricity demand and potentially shifting water use to power generation. Liquid and immersion cooling can remove heat efficiently at higher temperatures, but dry heat rejection gives very low on-site WUE whereas evaporative rejection retains high consumption.

reading_path.meaning: This section supplies the physical explanation behind the table’s contrasts. Its key distinction is between the technology that collects heat and the pathway that finally rejects it: liquid cooling by itself does not establish low water consumption.

Cold-climate siting allows free-air cooling that substantially reduces or eliminates mechanical chillers and evaporative towers, enabling very low WUE in Nordic facilities.

reading_path.location: Section 4.2, Natural water bodies as thermal sinks
reading_path.moves: Technical explanation; facility examples; ecological qualification; analogy to power-sector regulation; scalability constraints.

claims.text: Thermally coupling data centers to lakes, rivers, or seawater through closed-loop heat exchangers can eliminate consumptive withdrawals by using those bodies’ thermal mass.

support.text: Google’s Hamina seawater heat-exchange facility is described as its most energy-efficient center. Alibaba’s Qiandao Lake facility draws 17°C water from 35 m depth, achieves WUE below 0.2, and uses free cooling for over 90% of operational time.

claims.text: Natural-water-body cooling can expose data centers to forced curtailment precisely during extreme heat, when cooling demand peaks; climate change compounds that operational and financial risk.

support.text: The analogy is to temperature-discharge restrictions that have curtailed thermoelectric plants during summer heat waves, with projected mid-century European capacity reductions of 6–19%. reading_path.meaning: This option makes the distinction between consumption and ecological impact particularly consequential. The power-plant analogy adds a second limitation: a cooling method’s environmental constraints can become reliability and financial constraints under the same heat conditions that increase cooling demand.

reading_path.location: Section 4.3, Subsea data centers
reading_path.moves: Description of an alternative architecture; commercial example; inference from a discontinued demonstration; enumeration of risks and limits.

claims.text: Subsea facilities use seawater around sealed seabed server capsules as a passive heat sink, eliminating freshwater consumption.

support.text: China’s Hainan Underwater Intelligent Computing Center is described as the first commercial-scale installation, with capacity for 400–800 AI servers and WUE of zero.

China's First Underwater Intelligent Computing Center in Hainan boosts AI Development. https://news.cgtn.com/news/2025-03-26/China-s-first-underwate r-computing-center-boosts-AI-development-1C3kRAHnmSs/p.html #:~: text=China's%20first%20underwater%20intelligent%20computing%20center% 20in%20Hainan%20boosts%20AI%20development&text=A%20cutting%2D (accessed 16.11.25).

claims.text: Microsoft’s 2024 discontinuation of the technically successful Project Natick demonstration, conducted in 2018–2020, suggests economic or operational constraints.

Potential subsea impacts include thermal pollution and altered marine behavior, cooling-system noise, electromagnetic emissions, chemical leaching, and benthic disruption during installation and maintenance.
Initial assessments report temperature increases below 1°C, but comprehensive ecological monitoring remains unpublished.
High capital cost, complex maintenance, limited suitable sites, and underdeveloped regulatory frameworks constrain widespread subsea deployment.

reading_path.meaning: The subsea example extends the range of technically demonstrated freshwater avoidance. The author does not equate technical success with practical scalability, and explicitly marks the proposed explanation of Natick’s discontinuation as an inference rather than a confirmed cause.

reading_path.location: Section 4.4, “Waterless” systems and non-potable water use
reading_path.moves: Differentiation of water elimination from potable-water substitution; examples; quantified energy and cost trade-offs; economic explanation.

claims.text: Immersion or direct-to-chip cooling combined with dry heat rejection can achieve near-zero on-site water consumption.

support.text: ZutaCore’s HyperCool is described as completely waterless two-phase cooling capable of handling hundreds of megawatts; Deep Green’s immersion units capture 96% of waste heat for reuse.

citations.reference_entry: Zutacore, 2025. https://zutacore.com/(accessed 22.11.25).
Deep Green, n.d. https://deepgreen.energy/ (accessed 29.11.25).

claims.text: Treated wastewater and reclaimed water reduce pressure on potable supplies.

support.text: AWS has reclaimed-wastewater systems at 20 facilities, 16 in Virginia; Google uses non-potable water at over 25% of campuses; Los Alamos National Laboratory also uses treated non-potable water for its New Mexico data-center facility.

Holzle, U., 2022. Our commitment to climate-conscious data center cooling. ¨ https://blo g.google/outreach-initiatives/sustainability/our-commitment-to-climate-consciou s-data-center-cooling/(accessed 02.12.25).
Waldvogel, G., Hick, J., Tala, 2024. Los Alamos National Laboratory reclaimed water usage for data centers: a case study. https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/2433993 (accessed 02.12.25).

Operators face strong economic incentives to favor evaporative cooling because electricity dominates operating cost while water is generally priced below scarcity value.

claims.text: Non-potable systems require costly dual infrastructure and treatment; reclaimed supplies vary regionally and may compete with agriculture. Dry cooling performs worse in hot, dry climates where water scarcity is acute.

reading_path.meaning: The quotation marks around “waterless” are consistent with the distinction between on-site performance and lifecycle consequences. This subsection also makes the policy connection more explicit: the obstacle is not only engineering performance, but relative prices and the presence or absence of mandates.

support.text: The author cites work on northern European data-center waste-heat utilization.

Espoo, 2022. Microsoft and Fortum to collaborate in Espoo – Microsoft’s planned data centre region in Espoo will produce zero-emission district heating for Fortum’s customers in the Helsinki metropolitan area. https://www.espoo.fi/en/news/2022/ 03/microsoft-and-fortum-collaborate-espoo-microsofts-planned-data-centre-regionespoo-will-produce-zero (accessed 29.11.25).

claims.text: Waste-heat recovery provides computing and thermal energy from one electrical input, potentially reducing separate heat-generation demand and indirectly saving water when it displaces fossil-based heating.

support.text: A review of data-center waste-heat recovery is cited for the system-level benefit.

citations.reference_entry: Yuan, X., Liang, Y., Hu, X., Xu, Y., Chen, Y., Kosonen, R., 2023. Waste heat recoveries in data centers: a review. Renew. Sustain. Energy Rev. 188, 113777.

claims.text: Recovery requires proximity to heat demand, compatible temperatures, and seasonal alignment; it may not reduce on-site consumption, so lifecycle analysis is needed to establish net water benefits.
Most current examples are pilot-scale; systematic integration requires coordinated urban planning, heat-network investment, and policy incentives favoring recovery over simpler cooling.

reading_path.meaning: This option changes the unit of assessment from the isolated data center to a coupled urban energy system. The author preserves the distinction between a useful energy service and demonstrated water savings: the latter remain conditional on what is displaced and how the system operates.

reading_path.location: Section 4, concluding paragraph on three trade-offs and dedicated nuclear power
reading_path.moves: Synthesis; classification of tensions; extension to an emerging electricity-supply option; qualification.

claims.text: Three interconnected tensions constrain deployment: financial incentives favor cheap water-intensive cooling; dry versus evaporative cooling trades electricity and carbon against water; and solar-rich arid regions contrast with water-abundant northern regions that have less solar resource and partly rely on water-consuming hydropower.

support.text: The regional comparison again invokes hydropower reservoir evaporation as a water cost.

citations.reference_entry: Scherer, L., Pfister, S., 2016. Global water footprint assessment of hydropower. Renew. Energy. 99, 711–720.

claims.text: No single siting or technology choice resolves all three tensions simultaneously, underscoring the need for integrated assessment across water, energy, and carbon dimensions.
Several technology companies are exploring dedicated nuclear electricity, including small modular reactors, for reliable low-carbon supply independent of grid constraints.

Dedicated nuclear supply could reduce indirect water associated with fossil-grid electricity, but conventionally cooled SMRs would require cooling water themselves; net consequences depend on design and siting and warrant further assessment.

reading_path.meaning: The author consolidates the preceding examples into an integrated-assessment argument rather than selecting one winning technology. Nuclear supply is a new extension of the same burden-shifting concern, presented conditionally rather than as a settled solution.

reading_path.location: Section 5 opening and Section 5.1, first paragraph
reading_path.moves: Inference from technical review to governance; definition of digital water sobriety; market-failure explanation; awareness evidence.

claims.text: Limited deployment and scalability of technically achievable water-efficient infrastructure show that technology alone is insufficient; governance must establish accountability, standardized disclosure, and changed expectations of digital resource consumption.
Digital water sobriety challenges the assumption that AI expansion should proceed without considering water constraints.
Evaluating which AI uses justify water costs is urgent because public awareness is limited.

support.text: The author reports that 73% of UK respondents were unfamiliar with “digital pollution.”

citations.reference_entry: Tsoury, A., Barnett-Itzhaki, Z., 2025. Exploring the associations between socioeconomic and demographic factors and literacy in environmental and digital pollution. Sustainability 17 (14), 6336.

claims.text: Concentration in water-stressed areas reflects a market failure: siting is driven by electricity cost, latency, taxes, and land, while water prices omit local scarcity and environmental opportunity costs.
Companies consequently externalize the true costs of consumption onto communities and ecosystems, and this pattern will persist without regulatory correction.

reading_path.meaning: The governance turn explicitly draws on the technological constraints just reviewed. The three dimensions announced earlier—application evaluation, siting, and reporting—are restated, now with a causal account of why current market decisions do not sufficiently register water constraints.

reading_path.location: Section 5.1, paragraph beginning “To illustrate the first dimension concretely”
reading_path.moves: Normative comparison of applications; clarification against a binary interpretation; policy proposals; analogy and concession about implementation.

claims.text: Medical diagnostics, climate modelling, and pharmaceutical discovery offer broadly shared benefits that may justify substantial resource expenditure even in constrained regions; recreational image generation, automated marketing, and low-stakes queries have diffuse value difficult to justify against agricultural or domestic needs in stressed watersheds.

Digital water sobriety does not propose binary approval or prohibition of specific applications; rather, it advocates a graduated governance approach linking resource costs to demonstrated societal benefit.

Practical mechanisms could include scarcity-adjusted pricing, water-impact assessments for training above computational thresholds, facility water budgets tied to real-time watershed conditions, and preferential permitting for efficient cooling.
Analogous climate and biodiversity governance has encountered free-riding, jurisdictional fragmentation, and industry resistance.
Water governance may have structural advantages: locally visible impacts, existing water-rights and permitting institutions, and municipal control over allocation.
Effective digital water sobriety will nevertheless require sustained political will and enforceable regulation, not merely voluntary corporate commitments.

reading_path.meaning: The author gives substantive content to “societal benefit,” using a hierarchy of applications rather than treating every computation as equally justified. The immediate qualification is important: the proposed hierarchy is graduated and context-dependent, not a list of outright prohibitions. The governance analogies then acknowledge implementation difficulty while arguing that water has distinctive institutional advantages.

reading_path.location: Section 5.1, final paragraph
reading_path.moves: Qualification of awareness-based action; cited behavioral evidence; statement of underlying resource ethic; call for coordination.

claims.text: Awareness alone is insufficient; structural policy measures and educational interventions must be integrated.

support.text: The cited study finds weak correlations between knowledge of digital pollution and willingness to adopt sustainable practices.

citations.reference_entry: Barnett-Itzhaki, Z., Tsoury, A., 2025. From awareness to action: a UK-based study on public perceptions of digital pollution. Sustainability 17 (17), 7839.

claims.text: Fundamentally, digital water sobriety recognizes freshwater as a finite common resource requiring equitable allocation.
AI's water footprint results from deliberate policy and design choices, not technological necessity, requiring coordinated action across regulatory, educational, and industrial sectors.

reading_path.meaning: This qualifies the earlier urgency attached to public unfamiliarity: knowledge is not assumed to translate directly into action. The subsection closes by making its governing value explicit—equitable allocation of a finite common resource—and locating agency in institutions and design decisions.

reading_path.location: Section 5.2, Corporate commitments and accountability gaps
reading_path.moves: Assessment of voluntary commitments; example; temporal and spatial qualification; disclosure criticism.

claims.text: Corporate responses to water concerns remain inadequate despite growing awareness.

support.text: Google and Microsoft pledge water positivity by 2030, replenishing more than they consume in stressed regions; the author contrasts those promises with the limitations of replenishment credits and voluntary aggregate reporting.

citations.reference_entry: Paresh D., 2021. Google to replenish 20% more water than it uses by 2030. https://www. reuters.com/business/sustainable-business/google-replenish-20-more-water-than-ituses-by-2030-2021-09-09/(Accessed 29.11.25).

claims.text: Replenishment credits, restoration, and infrastructure investments fail to resolve the mismatch between continuous localized consumption and seasonal distributed replenishment.
Voluntary, unstandardized WUE reporting typically supplies corporate aggregates that obscure facility-specific impacts and prevent meaningful site comparisons.

reading_path.meaning: The article applies its local and temporal perspective to corporate promises. The previously reported reclaimed-water and Microsoft stress-region percentages recur as context, rather than new findings. The criticism is not that replenishment never occurs, but that its location and timing do not necessarily correspond to the actual consumption.

reading_path.location: Section 5.3, Regulatory responses and transparency imperatives
reading_path.moves: Report of emerging regulation; identification of an information barrier; specification of necessary disclosures; recommendation.

claims.text: Regulation is beginning to address data-center water use, particularly in stressed regions.

support.text: Virginia’s proposed disclosure bill would require annual reporting from major facilities in response to AI-driven growth; similar initiatives are described in Europe and the western United States.

citations.reference_entry: Barratt, L., Gambarini, C., Uteuova, A., 2025. Revealed: big tech’s new datacentres will take water from the world’s driest areas. https://www.theguardian.com/environme nt/2025/apr/09/big-tech-datacentres-water (accessed 15.11.25).

claims.text: Transparency remains severely limited because operators frequently withhold facility-level data as commercially sensitive, preventing reliable footprint assessment.
Comprehensive understanding requires facility locations, cooling configurations, and electricity sources, which remain missing or aggregated.

support.text: The author appends Jain’s citation to the statement about the information needed and its absence or aggregation.

citations.reference_entry: Jain, P., 2025. From bottleneck to breakthrough: AI in chip verification: how AI is transforming chip design with smarter verification methods. https://spectrum.ieee. org/calibre-vision-ai-chip-design (accessed 05.12.25).

claims.text: Standardized protocols and mandatory disclosure are critical priorities for quantifying AI’s true water impact and enabling evidence-based governance.

reading_path.meaning: The discussion moves from inadequacies in voluntary commitments to emerging legal requirements. Transparency is treated both as an accountability measure and as a prerequisite for knowing the footprint well enough to govern it.

reading_path.location: Section 6 opening and Section 6.1, Critical research frontiers
reading_path.moves: Recapitulation; research agenda; identification of attribution and lifecycle gaps; restatement of ecological and reporting uncertainties.

claims.text: Current facility-level accounting does not attribute water costs to particular models, training runs, or architectural choices.
Benchmark datasets linking workload characteristics and consumption across cooling configurations would enable targeted optimization and application-level decisions about justified water costs.
Indirect water in electricity and semiconductor manufacturing remains poorly quantified, particularly as grids adopt renewables with differing water intensities.
Integrated lifecycle assessment should incorporate spatial and temporal variation in regional generation profiles, as in agricultural assessment.

support.text: The agricultural analogy cites spatially and temporally explicit crop-production water-footprint work.

citations.reference_entry: Pfister, S., Bayer, P., 2014. Monthly water stress: spatially and temporally explicit consumptive water footprint of global crop production. J. Clean Prod. 73, 52–62.

claims.text: Cross-city evidence on district-heating costs, integration with legacy networks, and performance under different conditions remains limited despite technically viable pilots.
Disclosure protocols must specify measurement methods, temporal resolution, and geographic granularity to support governance and watershed assessment.

reading_path.meaning: The research agenda translates earlier limitations into work to be done. Ecological monitoring of lakeside and subsea systems, including the already reported 5–8°C warming concern, is restated as another of the five priorities. A new emphasis is attribution: facility metrics cannot yet directly support the application-specific judgments proposed under digital water sobriety.

reading_path.location: Section 6.2, Policy imperatives for water-sustainable AI
reading_path.moves: Consolidated recommendations; strengthening of siting controls; specification of reporting scope; system-integration incentives.

claims.text: Mandatory facility-level reporting should extend to on-site consumption, water embedded in electricity supply, and temporal variation.

New construction should be restricted in severely stressed watersheds, and concessions and permits should require cumulative impact assessment to avoid externalizing costs onto vulnerable communities.
Tiered digital-water-sobriety governance should link deployment to demonstrated societal benefit and local availability rather than computational economics alone.

Incentives for district-heating integration over simpler direct cooling would accelerate system-level solutions that displace fossil thermal generation and associated water use, providing energy, climate, and water co-benefits.

reading_path.meaning: This is a prescriptive consolidation, not a new evidence section. The pricing, impact-assessment, water-budget, and preferential-permitting mechanisms are repeated from Section 5.1. The siting recommendation now explicitly calls for restricting new construction in severely stressed watersheds, giving the earlier water-conscious-siting principle a firmer regulatory form.

reading_path.location: Section 6.3, The resource justice imperative
reading_path.moves: Concluding reframing; reuse of examples; attribution of responsibility; conditional future scenarios; appeal to political will.

claims.text: As AI expands, the central question shifts from marginal efficiency to resource justice: how much "intelligence" per liter of water is justified as both energy and freshwater become constrained?
The available technical pathways suggest that water outcomes reflect policy and siting choices rather than technological necessity.

support.text: The conclusion reuses Meta Luleå’s approximately 25 million liters annually as evidence that this volume suffices for hyperscale operations and China’s subsea installations as evidence of zero freshwater consumption.

claims.text: Computational infrastructure consuming public water during drought while agricultural communities face restrictions represents governance failure, not technical constraint.

support.text: The author returns to Colón as an example of siting that prioritizes electricity costs over hydrological constraints, disclosures that hide local impacts, and allocation frameworks that treat water as unlimited.

claims.text: Choices about AI location, cooling, and whose water it consumes will determine whether expansion worsens insecurity for vulnerable populations or stimulates integrated water-energy-heat innovation.

The speed of governance, accountability, and public-awareness development will shape the equity and sustainability of shared hydrological resources; implementing achievable water-sustainable AI requires political will before expansion irreversibly deepens stress in vulnerable regions.

reading_path.meaning: The conclusion returns to the article’s original distinction between technical possibility and actual deployment, now expressed as resource justice. Its examples are reused rather than newly established. The ending makes a strong claim about responsibility and urgency: the decisive constraint is presented as governance and political will, not a lack of cooling alternatives.

reading_path.location: Closing authorship statement, competing-interest declaration, data-availability statement, and references
reading_path.moves: Authorship attribution; conflict-of-interest disclosure; data declaration; bibliographic documentation.

claims.text: The authorship statement assigns the sole named author writing, validation, resources, methodology, investigation, formal analysis, data curation, and conceptualization roles.
The authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work.
No data was used for the research described in the article.

reading_path.meaning: The administrative ending adds no further substantive argument. The data declaration accompanies a review already described as synthesizing published figures rather than performing an independent footprint calculation. The references document the mixture of academic studies, corporate material, journalism, and technical sources described in the method.
